questions.q: What does CI/CD actually automate, building on Lesson 44's environments?
options: Writing KQL queries automatically without any human input
Enforcing that nothing skips from dev to prod without passing through test, without relying on a human remembering to follow that rule every time
Automatically generating new Eventstream sources
Replacing the need for separate dev, test, and prod environments entirely
questions.explain: Every commit can trigger a pipeline that builds, tests, and deploys automatically, in the same order, every time.

questions.q: In the example pipeline, why does the Deploy stage only run if the Test stage succeeded?
options: A broken change simply can't reach prod, because the pipeline itself refuses to let it — each stage gates the next
The stages actually run independently with no dependency between them
Testing is optional and only run for documentation purposes
The Deploy stage always runs regardless of test results
questions.explain: This is the entire point of staging — a failed test stops the deploy stage from ever running.

questions.q: What is Fabric's REST API, in relation to the Deployment Pipeline from Lesson 15?
options: A tool only for querying KQL databases, not for deployment
A completely separate deployment mechanism unrelated to Deployment Pipelines
The scriptable version of the same action — callable from a script instead of triggered by a click in the Fabric UI
A replacement for Git integration
questions.explain: CI/CD tools like Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions call this API as one step in a larger scripted process.

questions.q: Why doesn't "click the Deploy button" scale past one person?
options: Clicking a button is inherently less reliable than any automated process, regardless of team size
Fabric technically disables manual deployment once a second person joins a project
Nothing guarantees a second person follows the same steps, nothing stops a deploy without tests running, and there's no record of what happened and when
It works fine at any team size with no real downside
questions.explain: CI/CD isn't about distrust of any one person — it's about not needing to rely on anyone perfectly remembering the same steps every time.

questions.q: What triggers the CI/CD pipeline in the example YAML?
options: An Activator rule firing
A commit to the main branch of the Git-integrated workspace
A scheduled nightly timer only
A manual click in the Fabric portal, with no automation involved
questions.explain: This ties directly back to Lesson 15's Git integration — commits are what set the automated process in motion.
